citation: Li J, Soh KG, Loh SP (2024). The impact of post‑activation potentiation on explosive vertical jump after intermittent time: a meta‑analysis and systematic review. Scientific Reports.
population: Athletes aged 18–30 years (both sexes) from various sports (volleyball, rugby, soccer, basketball, track and field)
intervention: Post-activation potentiation (PAP) induced by squat, deadlift, or other high-intensity exercises followed by intermittent rest intervals ranging from 10 s to 24 min; countermovement jump (CMJ) height and peak ground reaction force (GRF) measured after rest
summary: This meta-analysis of 21 studies (327 athletes) examined how different rest intervals after PAP-inducing exercises affect explosive vertical jump performance. Rest intervals of 4 min and 5–8 min significantly increased countermovement jump height, while shorter (1–3 min, 10–15 s) and longer (10–24 min) intervals did not. The primary PAP induction method was squat-based exercises at 40–90% 1RM.
key_findings: Intermittent rest of 4 min significantly increased CMJ height (MD = −0.03, 95% CI: −0.04 to −0.01; P = 0.007).
Intermittent rest of 5–8 min significantly increased CMJ height (MD = −0.03, 95% CI: −0.04 to −0.01; P = 0.002).
Intermittent rest of 1–3 min did not significantly affect CMJ height (MD = −0.00, 95% CI: −0.01 to 0.01; P = 0.70).
Intermittent rest of 10–24 min did not significantly affect CMJ height (MD = −0.01, 95% CI: −0.02 to 0.00; P = 0.15).
Very short rest intervals of 10–15 s showed no significant effect on CMJ height (MD = −0.05, 95% CI: −0.16 to 0.06; P = 0.34).
limitations: Included studies were pre-post designs with unclear randomization risk; high heterogeneity (I²=98%) for very short intervals; only three studies examined 10–15 s intervals; subgroup analyses limited by small study counts.
